questions.prompt: Line ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, meeting AB at M. Point P is on ℓ. Prove that PA = PB.
questions.prompt_markup: Line ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, meeting AB at M. Point P is on ℓ. Prove that PA = PB.
questions.required_method: Use SAS on triangles PMA and PMB.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: AM = BM (M is the midpoint); ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB (both right angles, ℓ ⊥ AB); PM = PM (reflexive); △PMA ≅ △PMB (SAS); PA = PB (corresponding parts). If P = M, PA = MA = MB = PB directly. Alternative: the reflection across ℓ fixes P and swaps A and B.

questions.prompt: Point P is not on line AB, and PA = PB. Let M be the midpoint of AB. Prove that line PM is perpendicular to AB, so P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.prompt_markup: Point P is not on line AB, and PA = PB. Let M be the midpoint of AB. Prove that line PM is perpendicular to AB, so P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.correct_answer: PM ⊥ AB, so P is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.required_method: Use SSS on triangles PMA and PMB, then the linear pair of congruent angles at M.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: PA = PB (given), AM = BM (midpoint), PM = PM; △PMA ≅ △PMB (SSS); ∠PMA ≅ ∠PMB; they form a linear pair, so each is 90°; so PM is perpendicular to AB through its midpoint. SSS may be used here: in set 16 it was explained with SAS and a reflection, not with this converse, so the reasoning is not circular. Invalid: drawing the perpendicular bisector through P and assuming it passes through P (that is the claim).

questions.prompt: In a coordinate plane, A(-a, 0) and B(a, 0) with a > 0. Prove that every point P(0, y) on the y-axis is equidistant from A and B, and that every point P(x, y) with PA = PB has x = 0.
questions.prompt_markup: In a coordinate plane, A(-a, 0) and B(a, 0) with a > 0. Prove that every point P(0, y) on the y-axis is equidistant from A and B, and that every point P(x, y) with PA = PB has x = 0.
questions.correct_answer: PA = PB = √(a² + y²) for P(0, y); and PA = PB gives (x + a)² = (x - a)², so x = 0.
questions.required_method: Use the distance formula in both directions.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: both directions. (1) √(a² + y²) both ways. (2) (x + a)² + y² = (x - a)² + y² simplifies to 4ax = 0, and a ≠ 0, so x = 0.

questions.prompt: A(1, 1) and B(5, 3). Prove that every point on the line y = -2x + 8 is equidistant from A and B, and that every point equidistant from A and B lies on y = -2x + 8.
questions.prompt_markup: A(1, 1) and B(5, 3). Prove that every point on the line y = -2x + 8 is equidistant from A and B, and that every point equidistant from A and B lies on y = -2x + 8.
questions.correct_answer: For P(x, -2x + 8), PA² = PB² = 5x² - 30x + 50; and PA = PB simplifies to 8x + 4y = 32, that is, y = -2x + 8.
questions.required_method: Use the distance formula (squared) in both directions.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: both directions with algebra. (1) PA² = (x - 1)² + (-2x + 7)² and PB² = (x - 5)² + (-2x + 5)², both 5x² - 30x + 50. (2) (x - 1)² + (y - 1)² = (x - 5)² + (y - 3)² gives 8x + 4y = 32.
